lessons.title: Production planning and performance records
lessons.html:
Managing a piggery as a system

At supervisor level the focus moves from caring for individual pigs to managing the flow of pigs through the unit. A piggery works like a factory: sows are served, farrow, wean and are served again, while their offspring move through weaner, grower and finisher houses to the abattoir. Each house must be ready, empty and clean when the next batch arrives.

Batch farrowing and all-in, all-out

  • Batch farrowing - groups of sows are served in the same week so they farrow and wean together. This simplifies labour, makes uniform groups and allows houses to be emptied.
  • All-in, all-out - a house is filled with one batch, emptied completely, then washed, disinfected and left to dry before the next batch. This breaks disease cycles between age groups.

Key performance indicators

IndicatorMeaning
Pigs weaned per sow per yearOverall breeding herd efficiency
Farrowing ratePercentage of served sows that farrow
Pre-weaning mortalityPiglets born alive that die before weaning
Average daily gain (ADG)Growth rate in grams per day
Feed conversion ratio (FCR)Kilograms of feed per kilogram of live mass gained; lower is better
Post-weaning mortalityLosses in weaner, grower and finisher stages

Compare your figures with your own past results and with benchmarks from your feed company, vet or industry organisation. A worsening trend tells you where to look.

Records

Keep sow cards (service dates, boar or semen used, litter size born alive and dead, weaned), house records (pigs in and out, feed delivered, deaths and causes) and treatment records with withdrawal dates. Good records support culling decisions, feed budgeting and traceability when pigs are sent for slaughter under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000.

Example FCR calculation

A batch gains 6 000 kg of live mass and eats 15 000 kg of feed. FCR = 15 000 divided by 6 000 = 2.5. If feed costs R6 per kilogram, feed cost per kilogram gained is R15.

lessons.title: Advanced breeding herd management
lessons.html:
Gilt selection and introduction

  • Select replacement gilts from productive sows with good mothering.
  • Look for sound legs and feet, good length, at least the number of well-spaced functional teats required by your breeding company, and no hernias or inverted teats.
  • Bring in gilts early enough to quarantine and acclimatise them to the farm's diseases, as the vet advises.
  • Boar exposure helps gilts reach puberty. Serve them at the age, weight and heat number recommended by the breeding company.

Heat detection and service

Check sows for heat daily, ideally twice a day, with a boar nearby. The standing reflex is the clearest sign. For artificial insemination (AI):

  1. Store semen at the temperature on the supplier's instructions; protect it from light and heat.
  2. Inseminate at the right time after standing heat, usually with more than one insemination, according to the farm protocol.
  3. Use a clean catheter for each sow and insert it gently, with a boar present to stimulate the sow.
  4. Record the date, time, semen batch and operator.

Boar management

  • Keep working boars fit, not fat, with sound legs.
  • Do not overwork young boars; follow a service schedule.
  • Heat stress lowers sperm quality for weeks, so provide cooling in summer.
  • Boars are dangerous. Never turn your back on a boar, always carry a pig board, and never enter a boar pen alone.

Pregnancy and culling

  • Check for return to heat around three weeks after service; confirm pregnancy with scanning where available.
  • Feed dry sows to a target body condition. Too fat causes farrowing problems and poor appetite in lactation; too thin causes poor litter sizes.
  • Cull sows for repeated returns to service, small litters, poor mothering, lameness or old age. Keep a planned parity spread so the herd is not all young or all old.

Lactation

Feed lactating sows generously so they eat as much as possible, and keep the farrowing house cool for the sow while the creep stays warm for the piglets.

lessons.title: Growing pigs, herd health and marketing
lessons.html:
Weaner, grower and finisher management

  • Weaning is a big stress: new feed, new pen, no sow. Provide a warm, draught-free house, easy-to-find water and a palatable weaner diet.
  • Group pigs by size and avoid mixing later where possible, to reduce fighting.
  • Use phase feeding: change diets to match the changing needs of the pig as it grows, with gradual change-overs.
  • Environment control: monitor temperature, ventilation and ammonia. Watch pig behaviour: huddling means too cold; spreading out and lying in dung means too hot.
  • Prevent tail biting with enough space, feeder and drinker places, enrichment material such as straw or ropes, and good air quality.

Herd health programme

Work with the farm's veterinarian on a written health plan covering vaccinations, parasite control, biosecurity rules and post-mortem checks. Respiratory disease and diarrhoea are the main causes of loss in growing pigs. Strict biosecurity is essential because African swine fever and classical swine fever are controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; suspect cases must be reported immediately to the state veterinarian. Use antibiotics only on veterinary prescription and record withdrawal periods.

Marketing and carcass quality

  • Pigs are sold as porkers or baconers, depending on the market and contract.
  • Carcasses are classified at the abattoir, mainly on lean meat content measured by fat depth. Overfeeding finishers or slaughtering too heavy increases fat and lowers price.
  • Weigh pigs before loading to market at the target weight.
  • Withdraw feed before transport as the abattoir advises, but always provide water.
  • Load calmly with ramps and boards. Do not overcrowd the truck and avoid the hottest part of the day.
  • Check that no pig with an open withdrawal period is sent.

Using results

Abattoir feedback on mass, classification and condemnations, such as lung lesions, shows how well the herd health and feeding programmes are working. Discuss these reports with the manager and vet.

Key points

  • Batch farrowing and all-in, all-out improve labour use and break disease cycles.
  • Monitor pigs weaned per sow per year, ADG and FCR against benchmarks.
  • Select gilts carefully and manage boars for fitness, cooling and safety.
  • Control the environment and prevent tail biting in growing pigs.
  • Market at target weight and use abattoir feedback to improve.
